opus-5.5.text:
For me, the essence of task and motion planning is about bridging two very different kinds of reasoning that a robot has to do at the same time.

On one side, you have symbolic, discrete reasoning: what are the steps I need to take? If I want to make a cup of coffee, I need to grab the mug, put it under the machine, press the button, and so on. That's the classic AI planning problem, thinking in terms of abstract actions and their logical preconditions and effects.

On the other side, you have continuous, geometric reasoning: how exactly do I move my arm? Where do I grasp the mug so that I can actually place it under the spout later? Is there a collision-free path? That's the motion planning world.

The hard part, and I think the really interesting part, is that these two levels are deeply coupled. A plan that looks perfectly valid at the symbolic level might be geometrically infeasible. Maybe the way you grasped the mug makes it impossible to place it where you want. So you can't just plan the high level first and then fill in the details; the choices at each level constrain each other. Task and motion planning is fundamentally about searching over this hybrid space efficiently, figuring out which abstract plan is actually realizable in the physical world, and feeding the geometric failures back to inform the symbolic search.

What drew me to it, and also what motivated a lot of my work on combining learning with planning, is that classical TAMP assumes you have a very precise model of the world: known objects, known geometry, hand-specified action models. In the real world you rarely have that. So a big question for me has been: how do we keep the compositional, long-horizon reasoning power that TAMP gives us, while learning the abstractions, the models, and the skills from data, so the robot can operate in messy, unstructured environments? To me, that's where structure from planning and flexibility from learning really need to meet.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes symbolic and geometric reasoning and describes searching a coupled hybrid space, but does not say that TAMP decomposes an otherwise intractable search into local search problems.

r002.rationale: The response says choices at the symbolic and geometric levels constrain each other and that geometric failures inform symbolic search, but does not characterize connecting local search spaces as another search problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. To me, the essence of task and motion planning is really about bridging two very different kinds of reasoning that a robot needs to do at the same time.

On one side, you have the symbolic, discrete level: what should I do, and in what order? Pick up the cup, open the drawer, put the cup inside. That's the "task" part, and it's closer to classical AI planning: reasoning over abstract actions and their preconditions and effects.

On the other side, you have the continuous, geometric level: how exactly do I move my arm to grasp that cup without hitting the table, and where do I put it so the drawer can still close? That's the "motion" part, and it lives in a space of joint angles, poses, and collision checks.

The hard part, and what makes the problem interesting, is that these two levels are tightly coupled. You can't just plan a sequence of abstract actions and then hand it off to a motion planner, because whether an abstract action is even feasible depends on geometric details. Maybe the only reachable grasp on the cup makes it impossible to place it in the drawer later. So the task plan has to be informed by geometry, and the geometry has to be searched in a way that's guided by the task structure.

So if I had to boil it down, I'd say TAMP is about how you search over long-horizon, structured decisions while grounding every one of those decisions in the physical constraints of the world. It's the problem of making abstract plans that actually work when you execute them with a real body in a real scene.

What I find compelling about it is that it's essentially a blueprint for what we want from any intelligent robot: the ability to reason at multiple levels of abstraction and keep them consistent. The classical TAMP solvers did this with hand-designed symbols and explicit search, and a lot of my own work has been about asking how much of that structure we can keep while letting learning, from demonstrations or from large models, fill in the parts that are hard to engineer by hand.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes symbolic task reasoning from continuous motion reasoning, but does not say this decomposes an otherwise intractable search space into local search problems.

r002.rationale: It describes task and geometry as tightly coupled and jointly searched, but does not state that connecting local search spaces becomes another search problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the essence of task and motion planning is connecting what a robot needs to do with how it can physically do it. At the task level, you might say, “Pick up this object and put it in the cabinet.” But that assumes you can reach the object, find a suitable grasp, and move it into the cabinet without hitting anything.

Those decisions are coupled. A grasp that works for picking something up might not work for placing it where you want. So you can’t just decide the whole sequence of actions and then figure out the motions afterward. You need the physical constraints to inform the task plan, and the task goals to guide the motion search. That interaction between discrete decisions and continuous motion is really the core of it.

r001.rationale: The response describes coupled task decisions and motion constraints, but does not say that planning decomposes an intractable search space into local search problems.

r002.rationale: The response says task goals guide motion search, but does not describe connecting local search spaces as another search problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essence of task and motion planning is connecting reasoning about what to do with reasoning about how to physically do it. At the task level, you might say, “Pick up this object and put it in the cabinet.” But whether that action is possible depends on geometry: Can the robot reach the object? Is there a collision-free path? Does it need to open the cabinet or move something out of the way first?

So those two levels have to inform each other. A task plan gives structure to the motion problem, and motion planning tells you whether the task plan is actually feasible. The challenge is finding that connection efficiently, so the robot can turn a high-level goal into actions that work in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response describes task-level and motion-level reasoning, but does not say that planning decomposes an intractable search space into local search problems.

r002.rationale: It says the two levels must inform each other and that finding their connection is a challenge, but does not characterize connecting local search spaces as another search problem.
